name: Della Marchetti
languages: Italian (Calabrian, from her husband's family, and the schoolroom kind from the nuns)
equipment: Heavy coat: a man's black oilskin over a cardigan, the pockets full of spark plugs and union cards
Crowbar, short, kept under the seat of the Ford
Pocket revolver, a .32 that was her father's, in the oilskin's inside pocket
A 1919 Model T Ford truck with a homemade cab, bought from a Gale junkman for $40 and kept running on wire, faith and parts she steals back from the company garage
The secret books of Local 5512, United Mine Workers of America: one hundred and thirty-eight names, dues paid in real money, hidden in a feed sack under the truck bed
A tool kit, leather gloves and a rag that is never clean
A letter from the District organizer in Charleston promising help 'when the time is right'
features: Been Here Before (Survivor origin: advantage on initiative; when a fight or fright begins she always knows the nearest way out; once per long rest, rerolls a failed saving throw; the first time each scenario she meets a horror like the one she survived, the GM tells her one way it is the same. She was at the Paint Creek tent colony as a young woman of twenty-three when the guards' armoured train came through it at night.)

Hard to Kill (Roughneck: once per long rest, drops to 1 hit point instead of 0 if not killed outright; ignores her first level of exhaustion; advantage on CON saves against exhaustion, cold and hard labor)
Heavy Work (Roughneck: advantage on STR checks to lift, push, pull, break or force something, and she counts as one size larger for what she can carry or drag)
Bull-Headed (Roughneck, 2nd level: once per short rest, when she fails a fear check, she gains no Dread but must go at the source on her next turn, or break whatever is between them)

Trade: Teamster (Roughneck, 3rd level: advantage on Driving checks to keep a vehicle on the road or start a stalled one under pressure; she can get the Ford over the mountain to Gale in the dark with no lights, which she has done)

Grease Under the Nails (Mechanic background: she can fix the Ford, a mine motor, a pump or a generator, and a few minutes with any machine tells her what is wrong with it, including whether someone made it go wrong)

personality.traits: I talk fast, I swear in two languages, and I laugh loudest at funerals. I know everybody's business because I make it mine. I trust nobody new until they've done something for somebody else.
personality.ideals: One man is a check number. A hundred and thirty-eight is a union. The company wins by getting us one at a time, alone, at night, at the store window, in the office. So nobody goes alone.
personality.bonds: My husband Angelo, in the Gale jail for a killing he didn't do. Local 5512 and its book. Dewey and Vesta Spradlin, who I stood up for at their wedding last June.
personality.flaws: I think the company is behind everything, including the weather. When the union needs something I'll take it, and I'll use anybody, including you, and say sorry afterwards. I don't believe in ghosts, and I won't, even when I have to.

appearance: A sturdy, sharp-faced woman of thirty-eight with black hair cut short under a man's cap, olive skin, a broken nose healed crooked, strong forearms and grease to the elbow. An oilskin, a cardigan, a skirt over trousers for driving, men's boots. The Ford is never far away, and you can hear it coming for a mile.
backstory: Della Marchetti was born Della Kowalski in a Paint Creek coal camp in 1889, the daughter of a Polish miner, and was twenty-three in the 1912 strike, when the families lived in tents through the winter and the guards came through the colony at night. She married Angelo Marchetti, a Calabrian loader, in 1914 and came to Ottway with him in 1920. They have no children. She has driven trucks since the war, when there were no men to drive them, and she keeps the union's old Ford alive, carries messages over the mountain to the District office, and keeps the books of Local 5512, which officially does not exist: every man who signs the Ottway company's employment contract swears he is not and will not be a member of any union. On 26 March, the morning after Lester Gaither disappeared, Captain Kincaid's men took Angelo and Hobart Lilly out of their houses in their underwear, because they had argued with Gaither at the store that afternoon, and the sheriff charged them with his murder. There is no body. Della has been to Gale every day since. She does not believe a word of what Lettie Burchett hears under her kitchen floor, and she has not slept with the lamp off since Dewey Spradlin vanished.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Della is the union's face for the party and the engine of 'The Company and the Union' (campaignRules: Company and Union). She raises Union Trust and is how the party gets into Mount Moriah meetings, to Gale, and through the camp unseen. She is fiercely practical and will not accept a supernatural explanation until she sees it, and then she accepts it in one sentence and starts organizing against it: it is Della who first says 'it only takes them alone, so nobody goes alone', and she means the picket lines too. She carries CLUE B1 (the pattern: both men were alone) if asked to compare the two disappearances, and the truck.
dmNotes.voice: Fast, loud, profane, funny; Paint Creek English with Italian swearing she learned from her mother-in-law. Calls everyone 'honey', especially people she's angry with.
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: get Angelo out of jail. Secondary: build the Local until the company can't break it. Tertiary: find Dewey.
dmNotes.secrets: She knows Hobart Lilly was on the 1919 seal crew, because he told her the night he joined the Local, and that he joined because of it. She has kept it from the Local, because seven of the camp's best men were on that crew and two of them are union, and if it comes out that the men laid block while the others knocked, the Local will split. She is wrong about that, but it is her secret to be wrong about.
dmNotes.attitude: Toward the party: suspicious, then loyal. Toward Garland Hensley: contempt, which turns if he tells the truth about the night of 25 March. Toward Frankie Lowry: delight; she has read the Herald. Toward Dr. Ketterly: 'company doctor' is an insult in her mouth, until he does something for a miner's wife without charging the check-off. Toward Lonzo Cutright: wary respect.
